children: Leaders at Weil, Gotshal & Manges are discussing a plan to dissolve the law firm, according to a person briefed on the matter.

The discussions follow a continued exodus of many of the firm's highest-earning partners and failed merger talks that have left the once-storied firm in a precarious position. A wind-down would mark an extraordinary fall for a firm with some 1,200 lawyers worldwide that had been among the most well-regarded and profitable in the industry.

It is still possible the firm could change course. As of Tuesday evening, discussions had taken place only within a tight group of firm leaders and not among the broader partnership, according to people familiar with the matter.
A Weil spokesman said late Tuesday, "No decision has been made to dissolve the firm."

Weil has no debt and few liabilities, according to people familiar with the matter. It also continues to collect revenue as client bills come due. That relatively strong financial position makes a rapid wind-down remarkable.
Departing partners typically forfeit some earnings. Weil also repays partners that leave or retire their equity stakes over several years, according to people familiar with the matter.

The firm can dissolve without filing for bankruptcy. In that scenario, it would no longer exist. Its lawyers would need to find new jobs but could get paid at least some of what they are owed. Outstanding client payments would be collected and the accounts settled.

Among the firm's biggest liabilities is a roughly 380,000-square-foot lease at the General Motors Building across from Central Park in New York. Real-estate experts say the space is desirable and would likely be easy to re-lease, potentially for more than Weil pays now.

Weil's disintegration has stunned the industry. It has been losing partners for months, but an inflection point came in September, when Michael Aiello, its top dealmaker, decided to leave with his team for Cravath, Swaine & Moore.

To preserve its future, the firm tried to engineer a merger with Willkie Farr, a similarly sized competitor. The tie-up would have created an entity with more than $4 billion in revenue, better positioned to compete with the megafirms that now dominate the industry. Merger talks eventually petered out.

When the Willkie talks fell apart, more partners eyed the door, setting off a run on the bank. Rival law firms were receiving frantic calls from Weil lawyers wanting to jump. The drumbeat of departures continued.

Complicating the situation, Weil has been undergoing a leadership transition. Earlier this year, the firm appointed private-equity partner Ramona Nee to succeed Barry Wolf, who has served as the firm's leader for 16 years. Some firm insiders say there was a power struggle between influential partners who wanted to grow to compete with megafirm rivals and others who wanted to remain smaller.
In September, Nee told partners she didn't plan to take the leadership role.

Weil Gotshal, founded in 1931, was a pioneer among elite firms in building a restructuring practice, leading some of the largest bankruptcies in history, including Lehman Brothers, General Motors, Enron and WorldCom. It also has been a dominant force in public M&A and private-equity dealmaking.

The financial crisis and the resulting boom in bankruptcy work solidified its reputation as a restructuring force. But it was slower than some peers to reinvest in growing its business and cut lawyers when the bankruptcy work dried up, according to legal industry observers.

The firm's rapid fall reflects widespread turbulence in the legal industry, where respected firms can quickly become vulnerable if even a couple of their top moneymakers leave and take their high-powered clients with them. Weil made $2.1 billion in revenue last year, but its growth has been relatively stagnant over the past decade despite its blue-chip reputation.

Law firms are competing for top talent like never before and many are falling behind megafirms like Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins, which have the capital to invest in artificial intelligence and lure the best talent.
